Abstract
Flexible social comparisons require transforming information across reference frames, a process thought to depend on map-like computations in the hippocampal formation. Previous work has shown that egocentric social biases—an implicit reliance on self-knowledge—emerge when relative attributes of others are integrated into absolute social reference frames. However, it remains unclear whether this bias depends on the comparison being made in a specific reference frame (absolute vs relative), or on the type of social agent involved (individuals vs groups). Across two behavioural experiments, we employed a social coordinate transformation task where participants learned a stranger's preferences relative to either an individual or a group (relative frame) and then made inferences within an absolute reference frame defined by the alternative entity type.
